tool_summary: The Perl interpreter. Can execute a visible inline expression (-e), an opaque script file, or read from stdin.
platform_notes: Behavior of -e and bare invocation is consistent across Perl on Linux and macOS.

rules.description: The -e flag executes the given string as Perl code. When that string is visible in the invocation, commandant can inspect it directly. This rule fires when the payload itself contains a known destructive pattern (system()/backticks shelling out to rm -rf, unlink in a loop over a broad glob, etc.).
rules.notes: Coarse string-sniff over the -e payload, not a recursive re-assessment. See R-INS-05.

rules.description: The -e flag executes the given string as Perl code. The code is visible in the invocation and does not itself match a known destructive pattern, but any -e invocation still executes arbitrary Perl including file I/O, network access, and shelling out.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends on the executed code, which is visible in the -e argument and can be reviewed prior to execution, unlike a script file invocation.

rules.description: The -i flag edits files in place, optionally with a backup suffix. Without a backup suffix, the original file content is overwritten with no recovery path.
rules.reversible_note: Reversible only if a backup suffix was supplied to -i; bare -i overwrites in place with no recovery path.

rules.description: Invoking perl with a script file path executes the file's contents, which are not visible in the command string itself and cannot currently be inspected by commandant. Treated as the worst case since the script's actions are entirely opaque.
rules.reversible_note: Reversibility depends entirely on the script's contents, which commandant does not inspect. Treated as the worst case. See R-INS-03.

rules.description: Bare invocation with no -e and no script argument reads Perl code from stdin. Uncommon in an autonomous agent context.
